lesson.title: The Spanish-American War: A Nation Looks Overseas
lesson.summary: In 1898 the United States fought a brief but consequential war against Spain over Cuba, a conflict that turned the country into an overseas colonial power almost overnight.
lesson.body:
By the 1890s many Americans had come to believe their country needed new outlets for its energy and ambition. The historian Frederick Jackson Turner argued in 1893 that the closing of the frontier, the official end of open land available for continental settlement, marked the end of a defining chapter in American development, and some political and business leaders began looking overseas for the next one. At the same time, the industrial fortunes and political battles of Gilded Age politics had produced a country with growing naval ambitions, expanding export markets, and leaders influenced by theorists like Alfred Thayer Mahan, who argued that national greatness depended on sea power and overseas coaling stations.

The immediate cause of the war was closer to home. Cuban rebels had been fighting for independence from Spanish colonial rule since 1895, and Spain's harsh methods of suppressing the rebellion, including forcing civilians into crowded reconcentration camps, drew heavy coverage in American newspapers. Publishers like William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer competed for readers with sensational, sometimes exaggerated reporting on Spanish atrocities, a style of coverage often called yellow journalism, which pushed American public opinion toward intervention. Tensions escalated sharply after the battleship USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor in February 1898, an event covered in more detail as its own topic, which many Americans blamed on Spain even though the cause was never conclusively proven.

Congress declared war in April 1898, and the fighting that followed was short, lasting only about ten weeks, leading Secretary of State John Hay to later call it a splendid little war. Commodore George Dewey's fleet destroyed the Spanish squadron at Manila Bay in the Philippines on May 1, 1898, a striking early victory far from Cuba itself. On land, American forces including Theodore Roosevelt's volunteer cavalry regiment, the Rough Riders, fought at the Battle of San Juan Hill near Santiago de Cuba in July 1898, and the US Navy destroyed the Spanish fleet trying to escape Santiago harbor shortly after. Spain sued for peace, and an armistice was signed in August 1898. The war's outcome, negotiated in the Treaty of Paris later that year, transformed the United States from a continental power into an overseas empire almost overnight, raising hard questions the country had never really had to answer before about whether it should govern distant peoples who had no say in the matter.
